segments.text: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, vitamin D supplements in your heart. Another win for keyhole surgery in women. How things are changing in the resuscitation of newborn babies in the labour ward and also in the care of preterm babies. And jogging into a back. Most people will suffer an episode of back pain sometime in their lives, often more than one. It's a huge cause of lost days at work and medical costs, not to mention the disability that can be involved.
Now, you can find experts who say that jogging is poison for the back because it pummels the spine.
But a world-first study from Deakin University on the effects of jogging and running on intervertebral discs suggests otherwise.
The lead author is Daniel Bellavy, and he's in our Melbourne studio. Welcome to The Health Report.
Good evening, Norman.
So tell us about this study.
Well, as you introduced, the back pain is a massive problem for Australian society,
And it's the leading cause of disability and lost productivity in the country, even when you account for more deaths due to other diseases.
And in managing this sort of issue, what I wanted to look at was to see, can we find ways to, for example, strengthen the discs in the back?
And the conventional wisdom in the research field is that either you can't or if there is an effect, that it's going to be too slow to have a meaningful effect in a person's life.
And also there was no evidence, whilst there was some evidence in animals, there was no evidence in humans that exercise did make a difference.
Precisely. And the thing is that what might happen or be relevant in an animal mightn't be the case in humans.
And we're talking about the shock absorbers between the vertebrae, the bones and the spine.
Precisely, yeah. And as I said, the animals, this research has been done with them before, but their metabolism is a lot faster and also they walk into a force.
And whether that applies then to humans, it does not matter.
matter. So tell us what you did in the study. Well, what I decided to do is to look at certain
kinds of physical activity that we think are possibly going to be at the very worst,
not detrimental to the spine at high volumes, or that might be beneficial. Now, based upon this
work from animals and also from other studies we've seen before, I thought that examining
walking or running might be a good way to see if this exercise can actually improve the discs.
So you have three groups of young people, relatively young people, 25, 35, men and women
with varying levels of activity. Tell us about the varying levels of activity.
Well, we had obviously a group of people who didn't do any support, any sport at all. They
were healthy, right? There were no back problems at all, but they just were simply not involved in
any regular physical activity. And then we had a group of people who regularly run marathons,
so running at least 50 kilometers a week and doing that for at least five years.
And also a group of people who were regular joggers, so running 20 to 40 kilometers a week,
but, and also for at least five years, but also again, no other kind of sports. We just looked
at people who just ran, so triathletes and so forth, we didn't look at. And you did MRIs on
their backs. Yep. What did you find? So this is not a randomized trial, this is just seeing what
the effect was. Seeing what the effect was, because there's no data before it all in humans,
before you go off and do the randomized control trial, you need to see if there is any kind of
effect at all. And this is back in the studies of bone in the late 80s and early 90s, you needed
that first cross-sectional study between different types of sports or different types of athletic
groups to see if there was a difference. And that was then the justification to say, look, okay,
let's go off and do a randomized control trial. So what did you find about their discs?
Well, we found that the runners had better discs.
And most interestingly, on the one hand, we found there was more water and more hydration in the disc.
And that's indicative of a healthier disc.
And we also found in the marathon runners, and I was personally really, really surprised about this finding,
that their discs were actually bigger.
Compared to the size of their bones in the spine, the discs were a lot bigger.
And that's indicated that the discs actually got bigger in response to the loading.
And this is controlled for, because your muscles around the spine are going to be stronger and so on.
So if you control for all...
Well, not necessarily.
No, the muscles actually, there's no difference.
There's no difference between the different groups in their muscle size.
And yes.
And so this is a pure effect on the things.
But I thought there wasn't that much difference between the joggers and the long distance runners.
There wasn't much of a difference between the two.
That's true.
And that did surprise me a little bit.
I thought we might see, you know, a sort of a stepwise effect.
But looking at the data further, it seemed like there was, that they sort of,
sometimes you can hit a ceiling with how much of a response you can get from a tissue.
Like you can do muscle training as much as you want.
You will only get so far no matter how much you train your muscle.
It won't keep on expanding and keep on getting bigger.
So why this effect then?
So basically healthier, larger discs with jogging and running
and 150 minutes a week I think is what you said with the jogging roughly.
So what was causing it?
Was it the impact or what?
Well, of course, because it's a cross-sectional study, we can't be 100% certain.
But we had a detailed look at the people's physical activity, right?
And we quantified that.
And what we found is that it doesn't appear to be the actual loading or the loading on the spine from running or from jogging.
rather it looks like it might even be in that walking loading phase
or slow jogging activities.
So you describe this as acceleration.
In the paper, yeah.
In the paper.
So this is, you know, if you go for a jog,
certainly if you're me going for a jog,
you're not jogging flat out the whole time.
You've got to stop to cross the road,
you know, make a concession to motor cars and things like that.
So it's that slowing down, starting up
that seems to stress the spine and make the discs larger.
Is that what it is?
That we can't say, not from the data.
I mean, it looks like, well, I guess the key message that, that, um, that came out of the
further analysis was that it doesn't appear that you have to go off and become a marathon runner
to get this effect. You know, you don't have to, um, start jogging 40 Ks a week and keep doing it
for five years. It looks like. And it doesn't seem to matter whether you run on grass or concrete.
Oh, well, yeah. Well, that probably doesn't matter too much. Um, for this kind of a thing,
there's a lot of dampening of forces when you, you know, you might, you might feel,
feel more shock, um, forces in your lower leg if you're running on concrete, but by the time
that gets up to your spine, that's been dampened a lot.
I mean, we can't answer that question here.
So you're still not absolutely sure what causes it,
but it doesn't look, it's certainly not doing you any harm,
it does you some good.
And does this inform back pain at all?
Yes, it does.
I mean, the key thing about this finding for back pain
is that it helps us understand
what kinds of physical activity are good for the spine.
It's one thing to avoid things we know are risky,
but you want to be able to make things better.
And from the point of view of preventing back pain,
this is what I think this is important for.
I mean, whether, you know, you can treat back pain by going for a run,
that's another issue.
I mean, it's important to keep active when you have back pain.
It's very important.
But I view it as being very important for prevention to know, you know,
what kinds of physical activity do we need to do to be treating our spines well
and reduce the risks of getting back problems.
And do these 25-year-olds have clapped out knees because of the running?
No, no, no.
Yep, so that's another myth.
I mean, obviously, if you're going off and doing marathon running,
there's a risk of overuse injuries.
But, I mean, this was a healthy collective.
And, yeah, I mean, they don't get those.
They weren't all wrecks in the lower legs because of that or anything like that, no.
Fascinating.
Daniel, thank you.
We'll look forward to your randomised trial.
Okay, thank you, Noah.
Daniel Bellavy is an Associate Professor
in the Institute of Physical Activity and Nutrition
at Deakin University in Melbourne.
And you're listening to The Health Report on RN, ABC News
and CBC Radio across Canada.
I'm Norman Swan.
There have been suggestions in the past
that populations of people with normal
or high normal vitamin D levels
have lower rates of heart disease.
And that's made some experts argue
that vitamin D supplements must be good
for your heart and arteries,
rather than the alternate explanation,
which is that such people might just be out in the sun,
living a healthier lifestyle than the average person.
Anyway, there have been some randomised trials of relatively low-dose vitamin D
which have not shown any protective effects,
which is why a New Zealand group has tested high doses.
The lead researcher was Robert Scrag at the University of Auckland.
He's currently in London, which is where we've woken him up to talk to you.
Welcome to the Health Report, Robert.
Thank you. I say good morning, Norman.
Yeah, I hope you've had your first cup of coffee.
Thanks, Josh.
So tell us about this study.
Yes, well the study started in 2011.
Over a couple of years we recruited about 5,000 people
and then gave them monthly doses of vitamin D
or a very exactly similar looking placebo
and followed them up until the middle of 2015.
So it's the largest study to date on high dose vitamin D.
And it was 200,000 units you were giving them?
It was the initial bolus dose of 200,000
and then monthly dose that we mailed to their homes.
So that's equivalent to about 3,300 international units a day,
much more than what previous studies have used.
And did they take the vitamin D?
Yes, from the evidence that we had from the study,
we had very good adherence.
There was a subgroup where we did measure their vitamin D levels
and in that group we doubled the vitamin D levels in people that took vitamin D.
We also monitored that through questionnaires
and from the questionnaires that we had returned to us,
we estimated about 85% of capsules were taken during the follow-up period.
So very excellent deterrence and also very good retention in New Zealand.
Here we can link everybody through a unique number
to Ministry of Health Records on cardiovascular disease.
and mortality. So in effect nobody dropped out of our study because we could track what was
happening to the health status. Yeah the New Zealanders always do it better than us. So listen
and these were people aged over 50, average age 65. Were they at particularly high risk of heart
disease? Well in the high risk group from 50 to 84 the average age is about 66, 67 at baseline
and so right across the... So they're at high risk just because of their age?
because of their age it turned out that as happens in clinical trials they are healthier
than average so we didn't get the number of deaths that we expected um in this group but
this is pretty part of the course when it comes to clinical trial damage so people living longer
it's just really annoying isn't it and what did you find well um well it was a little disappointing
having spent a huge amount of effort on it but basically we didn't find any effect whatsoever
from vitamin D on heart disease rates and stroke rates as well
or right across the spectrum of cardiovascular disease.
So you looked at heart attack, stroke, heart failure,
whether you needed a stent, that sort of thing.
Yes, yes.
New people with people who had nearly diagnosed hypertension,
the full spectrum of cardiovascular disease
that the previous observational studies have shown
this inverse relationship with vitamin D status.
And so we didn't find anything in our study.
The effect was almost even in the two groups that we were comparing,
vitamin D and placebo.
We even looked into low vitamin D levels and didn't find any effect there either.
So if you came in with low vitamin D levels, it didn't make a difference.
So done deal, vitamin D doesn't help your heart?
No, no, no, it's not a done deal.
There is emerging evidence to suggest that daily supplements of vitamin D
might be more beneficial for other health effects
like particularly respiratory infection.
So I think we have to wait for the other big studies underway at the moment,
particularly there's a large study being carried out in the US
called the VITAL study where they're giving daily vitamin D.
And also there's a very large study being carried out in Australia
called D-Health being led by universities,
researchers from the University of Queensland.
So I think we need to wait for those studies to come in before we know 100% sure what's
going on with vitamin D and cardiovascular disease.
There certainly is evidence for other health benefits.
So I think in another three or four years when all the large studies currently underway
are in, we'll know what's going on with this hormone.
So don't sell your shares in the vitamin companies just yet?
Well, if I had any, I would keep on doing them, but I don't.
Robert, thanks very much for joining us.
I'll let you get on with your day in London.
Okay.
Thank you very much.
Robert Scragge is in the School of Population Health
at the University of Auckland.
Over 300,000 women give birth in Australia each year
and an astounding one in five of their babies
require resuscitation.
I had to resuscitate one of my daughters.
And according to one of the series of papers
in The Lancet this week,
I'd probably do it differently if it were today.
Then there are the 9% of babies
born who are preterm,
defined as being delivered earlier than 37 weeks gestation.
The average preterm baby in Australia is born at 33 weeks
and many require intensive care,
usually because of their immature lungs.
And things have changed there too in the last two or three decades,
according to another in this Lancet series.
But some things remain the same,
such as the spectre of a dreadful chronic lung condition
called bronchopulmonary dysplasia, BPD.
Two of the Lancet authors,
who are at the Royal Women's Hospital in Melbourne,
Join us now, Brett Manley and Louis Zohn.
Both of them are neonatologists.
Welcome to you both.
Thank you.
Good evening, Norman.
Brett, let's start with resuscitation.
You were the lead author on that paper.
You know, we used to sort of be terrified when you had a baby with what's called meconium aspiration,
where the baby had pooed in the womb and you breathed in and you'd run to it and suck the baby out.
But from your paper, it turns out I did it all wrong in my early days.
Well, that might be right, Norman.
It seems like a lot of areas in neonatology,
we've come full circle in our understanding
of how to treat some conditions of newborn babies.
And meconium aspiration is one of them
where we've gone from suctioning all infants
to try and get the meconium out of their earways after they're born
to now minimising the infants that we suction the meconium from.
And that gives you a better outcome because it's traumatic.
Is that what the story is?
Well, it certainly doesn't give worse outcomes.
And I think the less we can do, the better.
a lesson that we've learnt is that we really should be just getting on and helping these
babies breathe and not spending too much time trying to suction the meconium
from the airways. Because a lot of this, I mean, we'll come to just a few
of the things that you do. We don't have a lot of time, but a few things you do now that you didn't do
before. But it used to be when you had to sort of ventilate the baby and get
ventilating the baby with a mask is the other thing or
intubate the baby that you're suggesting now that you don't use oxygen, you use air.
Yeah, that's right.
Through the history of neonatology, as technologies have increased,
we've gone from having really no therapies to help babies breathe
where all we could give them was oxygen
through to now having a lot better understanding
of how we should help babies breathe
and also having much better technologies.
And as the years have gone by,
we've come to realise that oxygen is not a benign drug
and actually babies that don't need as much oxygen as we think we do,
it can do harm.
Such as?
Well, the recommendations now in term babies are that actually resuscitating babies in oxygen will improve survival.
In air, you mean?
Sorry, in air, that's correct, in no oxygen.
And in preterm infants, we've seen epidemics through history of oxygen diseases such as retinopathy of prematurity.
That's the blindness associated with too much oxygen.
And even just in the labour ward, so a short episode of too much oxygen can damage the eyes in these premature babies.
It seems that way. And so now we actually, when we're resuscitating a sick newborn infant,
all term and late preterm babies will be resuscitated in air. That's 21% oxygen.
The preterm infants, we're still trying to work out the best way to use oxygen,
particularly the very preterm infants born before 32 weeks of gestation. And it seems like those
very preterm babies do need some oxygen. And delayed clamping of the umbilical cord.
Well, another example of things going full circle in neonatology, there's a long history
describing delayed clamping of the cord.
But in recent decades, it's been much more common for the cord to be clamped immediately
after birth.
But now we're seeing the benefits both for term and preterm babies of delaying clamping
of the cord even by 60 seconds or more.
And I think that the potential benefits depend on whether babies are born in developed or
developing countries.
And for example, in developing countries, that little bit longer with some more blood flowing towards the baby might increase iron stores and help to reduce iron deficiency anemia.
And sometimes you can get a very oxygen deprived baby coming out and you're really worried about the baby.
And the natural inclination with a newborn baby is to warm them.
But in fact, making them a bit cold therapeutically is good for them.

Yeah, I think a very important advance over the last decade or so has been our use of therapeutic cooling, whole body cooling of babies who have suffered birth asphyxia, who've been deprived of oxygen and blood to their brain.

And we've seen that particularly for those babies that are moderately to severely affected that this cooling for several days and keeping the core body temperature low really does improve survival and other outcomes.
Louise Owen, less is more seems to be the theme in preterm babies as well
so what we've just been talking about with Brett
is usually often, not always, but often the full term baby needing resuscitation
but not exclusively, but in preterm babies
the general care seems to be less is more
I think so, as Brett has said, we've come a very long way
we've come a very long way in a very short space of time
we've gone from doing nothing to doing everything
to then actually the realisation that some of these things
there might just be a therapeutic middle ground.
So we've gone from being able to do nothing
to using ventilators on everybody,
putting tubes into their airways
and then realising that perhaps that isn't sensible for all babies
and there might be an easier way to support them gently
without further damaging their very delicate lungs.
Such as?
Such as just putting some short little prongs inside their nose
and using warmed gases that are humidified
with a little bit of additional oxygen if required
and allowing them to breathe themselves.
These babies are not born without any drive to breathe.
They can sometimes breathe very nicely on their own
with a little bit of support from us.
And can you make,
presumably you can make it worse with intubation?
Absolutely we can.
When we first saw the use of ventilation in premature babies
in the late 60s and early 70s,
we thought it was a fantastic thing to do
and babies did survive.
But we did pay the price with damaging their lungs
and saw a big increase in the babies
who had the chronic lung disease,
of boncopromy dysplasia you mentioned earlier.
And has that gone down over the years?
Because in your paper you imply that it's still pretty common
and you're not quite sure how to prevent it.
That's right. It unfortunately hasn't gone down.
So this is, I should explain here, this ends up with a child
who sometimes requires oxygen for extended periods,
doesn't have very good exercise capacity
and really can limit the first few years of that child's life.
That's right. It's a really important clinical condition,
very important for families and young children.
But what we found is that we've actually seen the rates rise over time
and part of that is because more of these babies are actually surviving
and babies who may have had chronic lung disease historically would have died
and we never saw it, whereas now these babies survive.
But they've also had to live through all the things that we do to them
and with them, for them, trying to keep them alive,
but can also damage their lungs.
And this less is more still true of extreme premature babies
who are 25, 26, 27 weeks?
It is.
We're still finding our way exactly how low we can go
and what the correct level is.
But it does seem to be so, even for these tiny babies.
What about other risks?
And you don't mention this in your paper
because you're talking about the respiratory issues.
But one thing that Brett mentioned was this retinopathy,
retrolental fibroplasia,
where you basically can get blindness because of oxygen therapy.
What's the story now with oxygen monitoring
and trying to prevent this eye disease?
that's a good question we've we've come from not being able to do anything except thinking a baby
looked blue and giving them unrestricted oxygen through to now having lots of simple non-invasive
ways to measure baby's oxygen we've gone from giving them lots of oxygen where babies survived
but lots of went blind through to the opposite where we restricted oxygen and babies didn't go
blind but more of more of them died because they had low oxygen levels to great big studies that
have been done all around the world trying to find the middle ground and we're still working
towards it and the oxygen guidelines are still changing we're still tailoring that
but a little bit lower than adult levels seems to be about where we're aiming.
Right and brain damage, cerebral palsy, learning difficulties?
These are still part of one of the things that we see in very pre-term babies and
due to a whole multitude of factors some of them from before birth some of them during their very
prolonged stay in the newborn intensive care units. And is less more giving you a better outcome
intellectually in terms of the brain function? I don't think we know that. It's very
multifactorial. There's so many things that play into that. Lots of things that can or cannot
happen to a preterm baby after they're born. Does the baby have an episode of very low oxygen? Does
the baby have an episode of bad infection of sepsis? So many things play into that over the time
that it's hard to be more specific.
Thank you very much to you both.
Fascinating and important news.
Louise Owen and Brett Manley are consultant neonatologists
at the Royal Women's Hospital in Melbourne.
Cancer of the uterus, the technical term is endometrial cancer,
is the commonest gynaecological cancer
and it's becoming more common in association with the rise in obesity in the community.
The treatment is surgical with the removal of the uterus,
hysterectomy, and the tubes and ovaries,
plus any involved lymph nodes.
And that can be done in two main ways,
an open operation via large incision or large-ish incision or keyhole surgery using laparoscopy,
the telescope. And while laparoscopic surgery for uterine cancer has taken off, there are
lingering doubts about whether it catches all the tumour and whether the complications are
problematic. Now, randomised trials are not very common in surgery, but to the great credit of a
consortium of gynaecological oncologists across Australia and New Zealand, a trial comparing
total abdominal hysterectomy with laparoscopy looking at disease-free survival has recently
been published. One of the organizers was Andreas Obermeier of the Queensland Centre
for Gynecological Cancer at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital. And Andreas is in our
Brisbane studio. Welcome to The Health Report.
Hello, Norman.
So this was early uterine cancer you were looking at?
Yes, that's right.
Do, I mean, what is early uterine cancer? I mean, there's a bit of controversy about
that, isn't there?
Well, we believe that about 80% of all uterine cancers are non-aggressive and are early, where we basically define early as the disease is confined to the uterus.
So tell us about this trial.
Well, we started this trial approximately 15 years ago, designing it, got a group together.
15 years ago?
Oh, that's the life cycle of a surgical clinical trial with follow-up of four and a half years.
We started this trial at the Queensland Centre for Gynecological Cancer with private donations
because we couldn't get funding for this trial.
There certainly wasn't government funding available.
We employed our first research nurse and collected data.
And with these data, we then were able to apply for funding.
And the funding basically made certain that we could see this through and continue this trial until we had the very first results available.
And as you are aware, the very first results were very, very good.
They were very encouraging.
They have shown that patients mobilized better, their quality of life is better.
Then we published data on complication.
So this is abdominal versus laparoscopy.
Absolutely.
So the quality of life was better with it, but the key was whether or not you treated the disease well.
We were dumbfounded by how much better laparoscopic surgery was.
We had an idea that keyhole surgery was better, but we were amazed by the extent of how better that was.
But there was always, as you say, this lingering doubt whether keyhole surgery would cause early recurrences.
And that really wasn't known.
and the paper that we published recently
is basically really good news for patients with endometrial cancer
saying there is no trade-off.
It continues to be good news.
There is no compromise in survival outcomes or in recurrences.
And what proportion of women reverted to the open operation
when you did the laparoscopic,
so they ended up with the open operation anyway?
That was very minor, between 6% and 10%.
Where, I should say, fairness, there is a study, a sister study, has been done in the United States.
And they had a larger conversion rate to open.
No, no, no, that wasn't the point.
But the point was that they had to do aortic node dissection.
And in really big women, that is very, very difficult.
and I think that cannot be achieved laparoscopically.
So in other words, if you go in and you find that it's not early,
you probably do have to revert to an open operation
to get the lymph nodes out well.
Well, as a matter of fact,
we try to stay with laparoscopic surgery,
but yes, there are certain situations
where you just can't push on laparoscopically, that's right.
And what about complications that keep gynaecological oncologists up at night,
such as pranging the ureter, which is the tube that comes down from the kidneys to the bladder?
Well, that was also very interesting because previous research suggested that interoperative complications
such as pranging the ureter or blood vessels or bladder or the bowel is more common,
which was not the case in our study.
So in our study, there was not an increased risk.
the risk of complications was exactly the same interoperatively.
However, what we also found that postoperative complications
were far less in the laparoscopic arm,
so down to 50%.
So the message for women is find a gynecological oncologist
who does the keyhole surgery,
or is that now pretty universal in Australia?
Well, in gynecological oncology,
I think most gynecological cancer units would offer laparoscopic hysterectomy.
But you're right.
I think women need to be educated that laparoscopic surgery is available
and they shouldn't settle for a total abdominal hysterectomy.
Andres, thanks for joining us on The Health Report.
Thank you.
Professor Andres Obermeyer is in the Queensland Centre for Gynecological Cancer
at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital.
I'm Norman Swan.
You've been with The Health Report.
Try and join us next week.
I'm your host.
